newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Vietnam forced labour campaign prompts concern.
newsitem.headline: Vietnam forced labour campaign prompts concern.

text.p: Vietnam's communist government on Wednesday stepped up its rhetoric on plans to breathe new life into a mass forced labour programme, prompting comparisons from economists with China's disastrous Great Leap Forward.

The party daily Nhan Dan called for the "the highest level mobilisation of people". Other newspapers detailed plans for the compulsory involvement of millions of people in infrastructure projects, including a north-south expressway along parts of the wartime Ho Chi Minh trail.
The English-language Vietnam News quoted Prime Minister Vo Van Kiet as saying: "I can guarantee (you) this will be a great construction site with the work of millions of people."
He added: "And we will certainly live again with the great and heroic spirit of the days when we cut the Truong Son Range to open a road for national salvation."

Vietnam has maintained a compulsory labour programme for many years under which young people are required to devote 10 days a year to work for the state, or else pay a fee of 2,000 dong (about 18 cents) per day for exemption.
But under proposals set to go before a National Assembly committee soon, the programme will be amended to increase the numbers involved by widening the age range of participants.
According to government officials, individual provinces and cities will set their own new exemption charges, meaning in effect that wealthier urban residents will pay more.

Both international and Vietnamese economists expressed concern over the plans, with one likening the proposed use of labour in vast infrastructure projects to China's misguided Great Leap Forward campaign of the late 1950s.
The campaign, at the behest of Mao Zedong, saw farmers abandoning their fields in a drive to produce steel from backyard furnaces. Millions died later from starvation.
"It's not in this size, not in this way, but the idea is the same," said a Vietnamese academic, who declined to be named.

"If the projects are small and closely related with the interests of the people, it's OK. If it's not well paid, not contracted, I think the ILO (International Labour Organisation) will be very interested," he said.
Others reacted to the news with surprise.
"We've been encouraging the government to mobilise labour at the commune or village level for small self-help programmes... (But) this overall thing is very surprising," said a Western economist.
According to Vietnamese estimates, construction of the 1,800-km (1,120-mile) north-south highway will cost at least $5.5 billion.
Unlike the existing National Highway One, the proposed route runs down the sparsely populated mountainous spine of the country, through pristine forests and jungle.

Vietnam News said the expressway would incorporate parts of the Ho Chi Minh trail -- a wartime network of roads and paths that Hanoi used to transport ordnance, supplies and troops to and from the U.S.-backed South.
Other Vietnamese analysts criticised the rhetoric, but cautioned against viewing the proposals with alarm.
"It reminds people of 30 years ago," said one. "It's not a very bright idea to use this kind of rhetoric, but I don't think anyone's too worried. It's different (today than) before."
